docs.title: HTTPX Limiter
docs.text: A lightweight package that provides rate-limited httpx and httpx2 transports.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
The package is published on PyPI. Plain pip install httpx-limiter installs only the shared core, which contains no HTTP client. Select the HTTP client you use with an extra, httpx or httpx2, and normally also a rate limiter backend, aiolimiter or pyrate.

pip install 'httpx-limiter[httpx,aiolimiter]'
pip install 'httpx-limiter[httpx2,pyrate]'

To use both HTTP clients in the same process, install both extras.

pip install 'httpx-limiter[httpx,httpx2,aiolimiter]'

There is no automatic fallback: you choose the integration explicitly by importing from httpx_limiter.httpx or from httpx_limiter.httpx2.

docs.title: Migrating from <0.7
docs.text:
The HTTP-specific classes moved out of the package root and httpx is no longer a required dependency. Install httpx-limiter[httpx] instead of httpx-limiter and change your imports. Rate, AbstractAsyncLimiter, and the limiter implementations keep their import paths.

-from httpx_limiter import AsyncRateLimitedTransport, Rate
+from httpx_limiter import Rate
+from httpx_limiter.httpx import AsyncRateLimitedTransport

The same applies to AsyncMultiRateLimitedTransport, AbstractRateLimiterRepository, and HTTPXAsyncHTTPTransportKeywordArguments. For HTTPX2, import them from httpx_limiter.httpx2 instead.

docs.title: Rate Limiter Backends
docs.text:
This package provides two different asynchronous rate limiter implementations to choose from:

  1. aiolimiter
  2. pyrate-limiter

Warning

While both implementations fulfill similar purposes, there are significant differences between them. Please read the descriptions below to make an informed decision about which one best suits your needs.

docs.title: 1. aiolimiter
docs.text:
• Single rate limit only: Supports only one rate limit at a time
  • Lightweight: Minimal dependencies and simpler configuration
  • Linear token refresh rate: As an example, if you set a rate of 2 per second, roughly one token will be added every 500 milliseconds
from httpx_limiter import Rate
from httpx_limiter.aiolimiter import AiolimiterAsyncLimiter

limiter = AiolimiterAsyncLimiter.create(Rate.create(magnitude=20))

docs.title: 2. pyrate-limiter
docs.text:
• Multiple rate limits: Support for multiple concurrent rate limits, for example, 10 requests per second and 100 requests per minute
  • Flexible configuration: Comprehensive configuration options
  • Multiprocessing dependency: Current implementation depends on multiprocessing which may not be available in all environments, such as pyodide
  • Stepwise token refresh rate: As an example, if you set a rate of 2 per second, two token will be added every second
from httpx_limiter import Rate
from httpx_limiter.pyrate import PyrateAsyncLimiter

async def main():
    # Single rate limit
    limiter = PyrateAsyncLimiter.create(Rate.create(magnitude=20))

    # Multiple rate limits
    limiter = PyrateAsyncLimiter.create(
        Rate.create(magnitude=10),  # 10 per second
        Rate.create(magnitude=100, duration=60),  # 100 per minute
    )

docs.title: AbstractRateLimiterRepository
docs.text:
Bases: RateLimiterRepository[Request]

Define the abstract repository for rate limiters of HTTPX requests.

This abstract base class provides a framework for managing rate limiters based on HTTPX requests. It maintains a cache of rate limiters and provides methods to retrieve request-specific identifiers and limiters.

Subclasses must implement methods to determine how requests are identified and what rate limits should be applied to them.

docs.title: Tutorial
docs.text:
You can limit the number of requests made by an HTTPX or HTTPX2 client using the transports provided in this package. That is useful in situations when you need to make a large number of asynchronous requests against endpoints that implement a rate limit.

Every example below is shown for both HTTP clients. Pick the tab that matches the client you installed. Transports, repositories, requests, and responses must all come from the same client: httpx_limiter.httpx works with httpx and httpx_limiter.httpx2 works with httpx2.

docs.title: Single Rate Limit
docs.text:
The simplest use case is to apply a single rate limit to all requests. If you want to be able to make twenty requests per second, for example, use the following code:

HTTPXHTTPX2 
import httpx
from httpx_limiter import Rate
from httpx_limiter.httpx import AsyncRateLimitedTransport
from httpx_limiter.pyrate import PyrateAsyncLimiter

async def main():
    limiter = PyrateAsyncLimiter.create(Rate.create(magnitude=20))

    async with httpx.AsyncClient(
        transport=AsyncRateLimitedTransport.create(limiter=limiter),
    ) as client:
        response = await client.get("https://httpbin.org")

import httpx2
from httpx_limiter import Rate
from httpx_limiter.httpx2 import AsyncRateLimitedTransport
from httpx_limiter.pyrate import PyrateAsyncLimiter

async def main():
    limiter = PyrateAsyncLimiter.create(Rate.create(magnitude=20))

    async with httpx2.AsyncClient(
        transport=AsyncRateLimitedTransport.create(limiter=limiter),
    ) as client:
        response = await client.get("https://httpbin.org")

Warning

Due to limitations in the design of the underlying leaky bucket implementation, which is used to implement the rate limiting, the magnitude of the rate is also the maximum capacity of the bucket. That means, if you set a rate that is larger than one, a burst of requests equal to that capacity will be allowed. If you do not want to allow any bursts, set the magnitude to one, but the duration to the inverse of your desired rate. If you want to allow twenty requests per second, for example, set the magnitude to 1 and the duration to 0.05 seconds.

from httpx_limiter import Rate

Rate.create(magnitude=1, duration=1/20)

docs.title: Multiple Rate Limits
docs.text:
For more advanced use cases, you can apply different rate limits based on a concrete implementation of the abstract AbstractRateLimiterRepository of your HTTP client, for HTTPX or for HTTPX2. There are two relevant methods that both get passed the current request. One method needs to identify which rate limit to apply, and the other method sets the rate limit itself. See the following example:

HTTPXHTTPX2 
import httpx
from httpx_limiter import Rate
from httpx_limiter.httpx import (
    AbstractRateLimiterRepository,
    AsyncMultiRateLimitedTransport,
)
from httpx_limiter.aiolimiter import AiolimiterAsyncLimiter


class DomainBasedRateLimiterRepository(AbstractRateLimiterRepository):
    """Apply different rate limits based on the domain being requested."""

    def get_identifier(self, request: httpx.Request) -> str:
        """Return the domain as the identifier for rate limiting."""
        return request.url.host

    def create(self, request: httpx.Request) -> AiolimiterAsyncLimiter:
        """Create a rate limiter for the domain."""
        return AiolimiterAsyncLimiter.create(Rate.create(magnitude=25))


async def main():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(
        transport=AsyncMultiRateLimitedTransport.create(
            repository=DomainBasedRateLimiterRepository(),
        ),
    ) as client:
        response = await client.get("https://httpbin.org")

import httpx2
from httpx_limiter import Rate
from httpx_limiter.httpx2 import (
    AbstractRateLimiterRepository,
    AsyncMultiRateLimitedTransport,
)
from httpx_limiter.aiolimiter import AiolimiterAsyncLimiter


class DomainBasedRateLimiterRepository(AbstractRateLimiterRepository):
    """Apply different rate limits based on the domain being requested."""

    def get_identifier(self, request: httpx2.Request) -> str:
        """Return the domain as the identifier for rate limiting."""
        return request.url.host

    def create(self, request: httpx2.Request) -> AiolimiterAsyncLimiter:
        """Create a rate limiter for the domain."""
        return AiolimiterAsyncLimiter.create(Rate.create(magnitude=25))


async def main():
    async with httpx2.AsyncClient(
        transport=AsyncMultiRateLimitedTransport.create(
            repository=DomainBasedRateLimiterRepository(),
        ),
    ) as client:
        response = await client.get("https://httpbin.org")

Tip

You are free to ignore the request parameter and use global information like the time of day to determine the rate limit.

HTTPXHTTPX2 
from datetime import datetime, timezone

import httpx
from httpx_limiter import Rate
from httpx_limiter.httpx import (
    AbstractRateLimiterRepository,
    AsyncMultiRateLimitedTransport,
)
from httpx_limiter.pyrate import PyrateAsyncLimiter


class DayNightRateLimiterRepository(AbstractRateLimiterRepository):
    """Apply different rate limits based on the time of day."""

    def get_identifier(self, request: httpx.Request) -> str:
        """Identify whether it is currently day or night."""
        if 6 <= datetime.now(tz=timezone.utc).hour < 18:
            return "day"

        return "night"

    def create(self, request: httpx.Request) -> PyrateAsyncLimiter:
        """Create a rate limiter based on the time of day."""
        if self.get_identifier(request) == "day":
            return PyrateAsyncLimiter.create(Rate.create(magnitude=10))

        return PyrateAsyncLimiter.create(Rate.create(magnitude=100))


async def main():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(
        transport=AsyncMultiRateLimitedTransport.create(
            repository=DayNightRateLimiterRepository(),
        ),
    ) as client:
        response = await client.get("https://httpbin.org")

from datetime import datetime, timezone

import httpx2

from httpx_limiter.pyrate import PyrateAsyncLimiter


class DayNightRateLimiterRepository(AbstractRateLimiterRepository):
    """Apply different rate limits based on the time of day."""

    def get_identifier(self, request: httpx2.Request) -> str:
        """Identify whether it is currently day or night."""
        if 6 <= datetime.now(tz=timezone.utc).hour < 18:
            return "day"

        return "night"

    def create(self, request: httpx2.Request) -> PyrateAsyncLimiter:
        """Create a rate limiter based on the time of day."""
        if self.get_identifier(request) == "day":
            return PyrateAsyncLimiter.create(Rate.create(magnitude=10))

        return PyrateAsyncLimiter.create(Rate.create(magnitude=100))


async def main():
    async with httpx2.AsyncClient(

docs.title: Transport Options
docs.text:
Both AsyncRateLimitedTransport.create and AsyncMultiRateLimitedTransport.create forward additional keyword arguments to the AsyncHTTPTransport of the selected client. The accepted keywords are described by the HTTPXAsyncHTTPTransportKeywordArguments type of httpx_limiter.httpx and the matching type of httpx_limiter.httpx2. Types such as Limits and Proxy must come from the selected client.

HTTPXHTTPX2 
import httpx
from httpx_limiter import Rate
from httpx_limiter.aiolimiter import AiolimiterAsyncLimiter
from httpx_limiter.httpx import AsyncRateLimitedTransport

async def main():
    limiter = AiolimiterAsyncLimiter.create(Rate.create(magnitude=20))
    transport = AsyncRateLimitedTransport.create(
        limiter=limiter,
        limits=httpx.Limits(max_connections=10),
        retries=2,
    )
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(transport=transport) as client:
        response = await client.get("https://httpbin.org")

import httpx2
from httpx_limiter import Rate
from httpx_limiter.aiolimiter import AiolimiterAsyncLimiter
from httpx_limiter.httpx2 import AsyncRateLimitedTransport

async def main():
    limiter = AiolimiterAsyncLimiter.create(Rate.create(magnitude=20))
    transport = AsyncRateLimitedTransport.create(
        limiter=limiter,
        limits=httpx2.Limits(max_connections=10),
        retries=2,
    )
    async with httpx2.AsyncClient(transport=transport) as client:
        response = await client.get("https://httpbin.org")

docs.title: Using Both Clients Together
docs.text:
You can install both extras, httpx-limiter[httpx,httpx2], and use both integrations in the same process. The limiters are independent of the HTTP client, so you may even share one limiter between them. The HTTP objects, however, are not interchangeable: an httpx_limiter.httpx transport cannot be used with an httpx2.AsyncClient, and a repository for httpx.Request cannot serve httpx2.Request objects.

import httpx
import httpx2
from httpx_limiter import Rate
from httpx_limiter.aiolimiter import AiolimiterAsyncLimiter
from httpx_limiter.httpx import AsyncRateLimitedTransport as HTTPXTransport
from httpx_limiter.httpx2 import AsyncRateLimitedTransport as HTTPX2Transport

async def main():
    limiter = AiolimiterAsyncLimiter.create(Rate.create(magnitude=20))

    async with (
        httpx.AsyncClient(transport=HTTPXTransport.create(limiter=limiter)) as old,
        httpx2.AsyncClient(transport=HTTPX2Transport.create(limiter=limiter)) as new,
    ):
        first = await old.get("https://httpbin.org")  # an httpx.Response
        second = await new.get("https://httpbin.org")  # an httpx2.Response

docs.title: Architecture Decision Log
docs.text: This log records the architecture decisions made for HTTPX Limiter, grouped by status.

docs.title: Accepted
docs.text:
• ADR001 - Use composition over inheritance
  • ADR002 - Provide one integration per HTTP client
  • ADR003 - Define the limiter and repository interfaces as abstract base classes

docs.title: ADR001 - Use composition over inheritance
docs.text:
• Date: 2024-11-22
  • Status: ACCEPTED
  • Author: Moritz E. Beber

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The rate-limited transports subclass only the abstract httpx.AsyncBaseTransport and wrap an injected transport and an injected rate limiter, instead of subclassing httpx.AsyncHTTPTransport. Each request is delegated to the wrapped transport inside the limiter's context manager.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: httpx separates clients from transports, and any object implementing httpx.AsyncBaseTransport can be plugged into an async client. Rate limiting is cross-cutting behaviour that should apply regardless of which transport sends the request: the default AsyncHTTPTransport, a MockTransport in tests, or third-party transports such as caching layers. It should also be possible to layer rate limiting with other wrapping transports in whatever order an application needs. Separately, the limiter itself is abstracted behind AbstractAsyncLimiter, so the transport cannot assume a concrete limiter implementation and is composed of two injected parts.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. (SELECTED) Composition
  2. Subclass the HTTP transport

docs.title: Option 1 (SELECTED): Composition
docs.text: Subclass only the abstract base transport and wrap an injected transport, delegating each request to it inside the limiter's context manager.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Adopted because: it works with any transport implementing the base interface.
  • Adopted because: it can be stacked with other wrapping transports in any order.
  • Adopted because: the wrapper stays small and easy to test by injecting a MockTransport and a limiter.
  • Adopted because: it composes naturally with the AbstractAsyncLimiter abstraction, letting the same transport work with any limiter backend.
  • Adopted despite: AsyncHTTPTransport's constructor options are not inherited, so create(**kwargs) has to forward them and type them separately (HTTPXAsyncHTTPTransportKeywordArguments).
  • Adopted despite: the wrapper must forward lifecycle methods such as aclose() to the wrapped transport, which also shares the inner transport's lifetime.

docs.title: Option 2: Subclass the HTTP transport
docs.text: Subclass httpx.AsyncHTTPTransport and override handle_async_request to rate-limit around the parent implementation.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rejected because: rate limiting would be tied to the HTTP transport and unavailable for other transport types, such as MockTransport or third-party transports.
  • Rejected because: it cannot be layered with other wrapping transports through composition.
  • Rejected despite: it inherits the constructor options and the aclose() lifecycle for free, leaving one object to configure.

docs.title: Supporting Material
docs.text: • httpx transports documentation https://www.python-httpx.org/advanced/transports/

docs.title: ADR002 - Provide one integration per HTTP client
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-11-07
  • Status: ACCEPTED
  • Author: Moritz E. Beber

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: HTTPX becomes an optional dependency. The HTTP-specific classes (AsyncRateLimitedTransport, AsyncMultiRateLimitedTransport, AbstractRateLimiterRepository, and HTTPXAsyncHTTPTransportKeywordArguments) live in one sub-package per HTTP client, httpx_limiter.httpx and httpx_limiter.httpx2, each installed with the extra of the same name. The package root keeps only the client-independent Rate, Number, and AbstractAsyncLimiter, and there is neither automatic client selection nor a compatibility alias for the old root imports.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: HTTPX2 is a separate package that keeps the HTTPX API but defines its own classes. Request, Response, Limits, Proxy, and the transports of one client are distinct types from those of the other. The two clients do not interoperate: an httpx.AsyncClient with an HTTPX2 transport, and the reverse, fails with an AssertionError, and calling a transport's handle_async_request with the other client's request does not fail at all, so only static typing catches that mix-up. Users should be able to install the library with either client, or both, without pulling in the one they do not use. The rate limiters themselves do not depend on any HTTP client. The package is still in beta, so a breaking change to the import paths is acceptable.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. (SELECTED) One sub-package per HTTP client
  2. Keep HTTPX at the root and add an HTTPX2 sub-package
  3. Select the HTTP client automatically
  4. One sub-package per HTTP client with deprecated root aliases

docs.title: Option 1 (SELECTED): One sub-package per HTTP client
docs.text: Move the HTTP-specific classes into httpx_limiter.httpx and httpx_limiter.httpx2. Each sub-package imports only its own client, annotates with that client's types, and raises a ModuleNotFoundError that names the extra to install when the client is missing. Code shared by both, such as the caching repository logic, lives in private, client-independent modules in the package root.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Adopted because: users install only the client they use, and the core imports no HTTP client at all.
  • Adopted because: each integration is typed with its own client's classes, so type checkers reject mixing an HTTPX transport, request, or repository with HTTPX2 and vice versa.
  • Adopted because: both integrations can be used in the same process, and limiters can be shared between them.
  • Adopted because: both clients are treated symmetrically, so adding or dropping a client later does not move the other one.
  • Adopted despite: it is a breaking change, and every user must change the imports of the HTTP-specific classes and select an extra.
  • Adopted despite: the public classes exist twice under the same names, once per sub-package.

docs.title: Option 2: Keep HTTPX at the root and add an HTTPX2 sub-package
docs.text: Keep httpx as a required dependency and the HTTPX classes in the package root, and add only httpx_limiter.httpx2.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rejected because: HTTPX2 users would still have to install HTTPX.
  • Rejected because: the two clients would be exposed asymmetrically, with one at the root and one in a sub-package.
  • Rejected despite: existing imports would keep working without changes.

docs.title: Option 3: Select the HTTP client automatically
docs.text: Expose one set of classes in the root that use whichever client is installed, falling back from one to the other.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rejected because: the choice is ambiguous when both clients are installed, and the result depends on the environment instead of the code.
  • Rejected because: the classes cannot be annotated with one client's types, so mix-ups would only fail at runtime, if at all.
  • Rejected despite: users would not need to choose an import path.

docs.title: Option 4: One sub-package per HTTP client with deprecated root aliases
docs.text: Use the sub-packages from option 1, but keep the old root imports as aliases that issue a deprecation warning.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rejected because: the root aliases must import a specific client, so they fail with a ModuleNotFoundError when the HTTPX extra is not installed, or need a lazy module __getattr__ that complicates the core.
  • Rejected because: the package is in beta, and a clean break is simpler for users and maintainers than a deprecation period.
  • Rejected despite: existing code would keep working for a transition period.

docs.title: Supporting Material
docs.text:
• Pull request introducing the integrations https://github.com/Midnighter/httpx-limiter/pull/417
  • HTTPX2 on PyPI https://pypi.org/project/httpx2/

docs.title: ADR003 - Define the limiter and repository interfaces as abstract base classes
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-11-07
  • Status: ACCEPTED
  • Author: Moritz E. Beber

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The limiter interface AbstractAsyncLimiter and the rate limiter repository stay abstract base classes instead of becoming typing.Protocols. Supported limiters are explicit: this package ships a subclass of AbstractAsyncLimiter for each limiter backend it supports. The internal, generic RateLimiterRepository[RequestT] implements the caching get method, and each HTTP integration exposes a subclass, AbstractRateLimiterRepository, that users subclass to implement get_identifier and create for their client's requests.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The transports enter a limiter as an asynchronous context manager around each request, and AsyncMultiRateLimitedTransport asks a repository for the limiter of each request. A repository decides how to identify a request and which limiter to create for it, and it must return the same limiter for the same identifier so that requests sharing a limit share its state. Limiter backends, such as aiolimiter and pyrate-limiter, are optional dependencies that this package wraps in AiolimiterAsyncLimiter and PyrateAsyncLimiter, which also translate a Rate into the backend's configuration. With the introduction of one integration per HTTP client (ADR002), the repository became generic over the request type, which prompted the question whether structural Protocols, possibly runtime_checkable, would be better interfaces than nominal abstract base classes.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. (SELECTED) Abstract base classes
  2. Protocols with runtime checks

docs.title: Option 1 (SELECTED): Abstract base classes
docs.text: Keep AbstractAsyncLimiter as an ABC with an abstract __aenter__ and a default __aexit__. Keep RateLimiterRepository as a generic ABC with abstract get_identifier and create methods and a concrete, caching get method that subclasses inherit.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Adopted because: support for a limiter backend is explicit, since this package ships and wraps each supported limiter, and the wrapper translates a Rate into the backend's configuration.
  • Adopted because: every repository inherits one correct caching implementation, so users only implement how to identify a request and which limiter to create.
  • Adopted because: instantiating a subclass that misses an abstract method fails immediately with a TypeError that names the missing method.
  • Adopted despite: a limiter or repository from elsewhere with matching methods, such as aiolimiter.AsyncLimiter, cannot be used without a subclass.

docs.title: Option 2: Protocols with runtime checks
docs.text: Define both interfaces as runtime_checkable Protocols, generic over the request type for the repository, and accept any object that matches them. A trial showed that the existing limiter subclasses keep working unchanged when they inherit from such a protocol explicitly, and that mypy, ty, and pyrefly accept aiolimiter.AsyncLimiter passed directly.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rejected because: a limiter protocol matches any asynchronous context manager, such as asyncio.Semaphore or asyncio.timeout(), so whether an object is a rate limiter would only be a convention.
  • Rejected because: a repository protocol does not share the caching get implementation with classes that only match it structurally, so every implementation would have to cache correctly itself, or the caching would have to move into the transport.
  • Rejected because: isinstance checks against a runtime_checkable protocol only test that the methods exist, not their signatures or the request type, so the runtime check gives little safety beyond what static typing already provides.
  • Rejected because: an incomplete implementation that does not inherit from the protocol is only detected by a type checker or when the missing method is called, not when the object is created.
  • Rejected despite: any object with matching methods would work without inheriting from the library, which decouples user code and simplifies test doubles.

docs.title: Supporting Material
docs.text:
• typing.Protocol and runtime_checkable https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Protocol
  • abc module https://docs.python.org/3/library/abc.html

docs.title: How-To Dynamically Adjust The Rate Limit?
docs.text:
The examples are shown for HTTPX and HTTPX2. If a server responds with rate limit headers, like X-RateLimit-Remaining, you can use a custom repository to dynamically adjust your client's behavior. This demonstrates the flexibility of the project's repository pattern by creating a repository that can be updated based on server feedback.

Warning

This pattern maintains a single global rate limiter that gets replaced when the rate needs to change. This works well for single domain or endpoint scenarios. For multiple endpoints with different limits, consider storing rates per identifier.

HTTPXHTTPX2 
import httpx
from httpx_limiter import Rate
from httpx_limiter.httpx import (
    AbstractRateLimiterRepository,
    AsyncMultiRateLimitedTransport,
)
from httpx_limiter.aiolimiter import AiolimiterAsyncLimiter


class AdaptiveRepository(AbstractRateLimiterRepository):
    """Adjust rate limiting based on server response headers."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self._current_magnitude = 5

    def get_identifier(self, request: httpx.Request) -> str:
        return "global"

    def create(self, request: httpx.Request) -> AiolimiterAsyncLimiter:
        return AiolimiterAsyncLimiter.create(
            Rate.create(magnitude=self._current_magnitude)
        )

    def update_from_header(self, remaining: int) -> None:
        """Adjust rate based on server feedback."""
        new_magnitude = 1 if remaining < 10 else 5

        if new_magnitude != self._current_magnitude:
            self._current_magnitude = new_magnitude
            self._limiters.clear()


repo = AdaptiveRepository()


async def rate_limit_hook(response: httpx.Response) -> None:
    """Inspect headers and update the limiter."""
    remaining = response.headers.get("X-RateLimit-Remaining")
    if remaining:
        repo.update_from_header(int(remaining))


async def main() -> None:
    event_hooks = {"response": [rate_limit_hook]}

    async with httpx.AsyncClient(
        transport=AsyncMultiRateLimitedTransport.create(repository=repo),
        event_hooks=event_hooks,
    ) as client:
        response = await client.get("https://api.github.com/users/octocat")
        print(response.json())

import httpx2
from httpx_limiter import Rate
from httpx_limiter.httpx2 import (
    AbstractRateLimiterRepository,
    AsyncMultiRateLimitedTransport,
)
from httpx_limiter.aiolimiter import AiolimiterAsyncLimiter


class AdaptiveRepository(AbstractRateLimiterRepository):
    """Adjust rate limiting based on server response headers."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self._current_magnitude = 5

    def get_identifier(self, request: httpx2.Request) -> str:
        return "global"

    def create(self, request: httpx2.Request) -> AiolimiterAsyncLimiter:
        return AiolimiterAsyncLimiter.create(
            Rate.create(magnitude=self._current_magnitude)
        )

    def update_from_header(self, remaining: int) -> None:
        """Adjust rate based on server feedback."""
        new_magnitude = 1 if remaining < 10 else 5

        if new_magnitude != self._current_magnitude:
            self._current_magnitude = new_magnitude
            self._limiters.clear()


repo = AdaptiveRepository()


async def rate_limit_hook(response: httpx2.Response) -> None:
    """Inspect headers and update the limiter."""
    remaining = response.headers.get("X-RateLimit-Remaining")
    if remaining:
        repo.update_from_header(int(remaining))


async def main() -> None:
    event_hooks = {"response": [rate_limit_hook]}

    async with httpx2.AsyncClient(
        transport=AsyncMultiRateLimitedTransport.create(repository=repo),
        event_hooks=event_hooks,
    ) as client:
        response = await client.get("https://api.github.com/users/octocat")
        print(response.json())

This is a fairly basic example. For real scenarios, you likely want to implement a global lock in the update_from_header method to avoid race conditions when updating the rate from multiple concurrent requests.

docs.title: How-To Combine Rate Limiting with Automatic Retries?
docs.text:
Even with a rate limiter, you may occasionally receive 429 Too Many Requests HTTP errors if the server's capacity fluctuates or if you have multiple clients running. A local rate limiter is your first line of defense, but it cannot guarantee that you won't reach a server-side limit. The solution is to combine rate limiting with automatic retries.

When you combine both techniques, it makes sense for the inner layer to be the rate limiter, while the outer layer handles retries. This way, each retry attempt is also subject to rate limiting.

docs.title: Using httpx-tenacity
docs.text:
Note

This recipe works with HTTPX only. httpx-tenacity currently supports only HTTPX and not HTTPX2, so there is no HTTPX2 version of this example yet. The rate-limited transports of httpx_limiter.httpx2 can be wrapped by any retrying transport that is built on httpx2.AsyncBaseTransport.

For this example, we use the companion package httpx-tenacity which provides a clean HTTPX transport-based approach to retrying. It also comes with sensible defaults that retry on server-side errors.

import httpx
from httpx_limiter import Rate
from httpx_limiter.httpx import AsyncRateLimitedTransport
from httpx_limiter.aiolimiter import AiolimiterAsyncLimiter
from httpx_tenacity import AsyncTenaciousTransport


async def main() -> None:
    retry = AsyncTenaciousTransport.create(
        max_attempts=3,
        min_wait_seconds=0.1,
        max_wait_seconds=0.5,
    )
    retry.transport = AsyncRateLimitedTransport.create(
        limiter=AiolimiterAsyncLimiter.create(Rate.create(magnitude=10))
    )
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(transport=retry) as client:
        response = await client.get("https://api.example.com/data")
        print(response.json())

docs.title: How-To Apply Per-Domain Rate Limits
docs.text:
When scraping multiple domains, you often need to apply different rate limits for each. This recipe shows how to configure domain-specific limits with a fallback default. Pick the tab for the HTTP client you installed.

HTTPXHTTPX2 
import httpx
from httpx_limiter import Rate
from httpx_limiter.httpx import (
    AbstractRateLimiterRepository,
    AsyncMultiRateLimitedTransport,
)
from httpx_limiter.pyrate import PyrateAsyncLimiter


DOMAIN_RATES: dict[str, Rate] = {
    "api.github.com": Rate.create(magnitude=30),
    "api.twitter.com": Rate.create(magnitude=15),
}
DEFAULT_RATE = Rate.create(magnitude=5)


class PerDomainRepository(AbstractRateLimiterRepository):
    """Apply preconfigured rate limits per domain."""

    def get_identifier(self, request: httpx.Request) -> str:
        return str(request.url.host)

    def create(self, request: httpx.Request) -> PyrateAsyncLimiter:
        host = str(request.url.host)
        rate = DOMAIN_RATES.get(host, DEFAULT_RATE)
        return PyrateAsyncLimiter.create(rate)


async def main() -> None:
    transport = AsyncMultiRateLimitedTransport.create(
        repository=PerDomainRepository(),
    )
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(transport=transport) as client:
        await client.get("https://api.github.com/users/octocat")
        await client.get("https://api.twitter.com/2/users/me")
        await client.get("https://other-api.example.com/data")

import httpx2

DOMAIN_RATES: dict[str, Rate] = {

DEFAULT_RATE = Rate.create(magnitude=5)

Of course, you may even combine this with the adaptive rate limiting technique.
